articles.title: Judge keeps immigrant delivery driver shot by ICE in custody for alleged assault
articles.summary: Prosecutors presented a video from cameras at a nearby business but the shooting of Wilber Garcés Pérez was not captured on the footage shared in court.
articles.body: AUSTIN, Texas — A Venezuelan delivery driver who was shot in his car by a federal immigration agent in Texas will remain in custody on charges that he assaulted an officer while trying to evade arrest, a federal judge ruled Wednesday. Judge Dustin Howell said that the case against Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, should proceed after prosecutors presented body-worn camera footage of the encounter in Austin, in which Garcés Pérez allegedly struck a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer with his driver’s side mirror. Garcés Pérez is charged with one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer and faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted. His case has sparked widespread outrage across the Texas capital city and brought renewed criticism from Democrats of President Donald Trump’s aggressive crackdown on immigration. With a bullet still lodged in his back, Garcés Pérez appeared in court in a wheelchair. His attorneys said he still urgently needs medical care, 10 days after being shot. He also wore a sling on his arm and needed help putting on a headset to listen to a translation of the proceedings. The defense called the charges against Garcés Pérez “retaliation” and argued that the camera footage was inconclusive because it didn’t fully capture the moment when he allegedly tried to flee. The hearing also included testimony from Homeland Security Investigations Special Agent Rick Bazan, who signed the criminal complaint charging Garcés Pérez with assault. The defense argued that Bazan, whose agency is the investigative arm of ICE, could not confirm whether the ICE agent was actually hit by the car mirror since no federal investigators interviewed the agent directly. Bazan also couldn’t explain why the officer allegedly struck by the mirror was not wearing a body-worn camera. Footage provided Wednesday in court shows officers pulling Garcés Pérez over Sept. 20 in Austin, where he was making deliveries for DoorDash. The video showed Garcés Pérez giving officers his drivers license through a crack in his window and then asking in Spanish if he can park his car so that a relative could come retrieve it. The officer demanded Garcés Pérez get out of the car multiple times, to which he asked if he could park his own car so a family member could come retrieve it. After a back and forth, Garcés Pérez abruptly and rapidly drives off. Prosecutors show video but not of the shooting itself Prosecutors presented a video from cameras at a nearby business showing the ensuing high-speed chase through residential streets. The shooting itself was not captured on the footage shared in court. The federal officer who shot Garcés Pérez wasn’t wearing a body-worn camera. The immigration officer who did have a camera was driving in a separate car and turned the camera off during the pursuit. Garcés Pérez said he was struck by a law enforcement SUV and spun around before he was shot. Federal officers told investigators, however, that Garcés Pérez attempted to strike an officer with his car at the end of the chase before the unidentified officer fired his weapon. The accusations against Garcés Pérez recall previous claims made by immigration agents after other high-profile shootings similarly accusing drivers of weaponizing their vehicles. In a handful of cases, the allegations have been undermined or walked back after the release of body-worn camera footage, drawing renewed scrutiny about the DHS’s reliance on vehicular stops to execute arrests. Lawyer accuses ICE of denying him medical treatment Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, one of Garcés Pérez’s immigration attorneys, accused ICE of denying him medical treatment for his bullet wound. “ICE’s conduct has been so egregious, that physicians, nurses, medical ethicists and health advocates have come together to demand his release,” she said outside court after the hearing. Garcés Pérez entered the U.S. in 2024 using CBP One, a program begun under President Joe Biden that allowed migrants to schdule appointments with U.S. authorities to be considered for asylum. President Donald Trump ended the program on his first day back in office. Garcés Pérez was an asylum seeker and had a valid work permit, according to his lawyer. She said a judge later issued a deportation order after Garcés Pérez missed an immigration court hearing because the notice had been sent to a former address. Judge Howell said he denied Garcés Pérez bond on the basis that he could be a flight risk to Venezuela, where he has a child. His attorneys have filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent his removal from the U.S.

articles.title: French high school students set fires, clash with police in anger over school conditions
articles.summary: High school students across France set fires and clashed with police on Wednesday and Thursday, escalating nearly a week of disruption.
articles.body: High school students across France set fires and clashed with police on Wednesday and Thursday, escalating nearly a week of disruption. Some 625 people – mostly young – were detained by police on Wednesday, France’s interior minister Laurent Nunez said, adding that 83 police officers had been injured. Government figures put the number of students and teaching staff injured during the days-long protests at 159, including one student who lost part of the use of his hand after setting off a firework. Videos also surfaced allegedly showing two teachers being attacked by students, provoking condemnation from the French president and officials as well as teaching unions. Protests began at some French schools last week but picked up Tuesday, with violent scenes overshadowing a nationwide day of protests by unions, workers and students against the upcoming government budget. The situation outside high schools worsened into Wednesday. On Thursday, clashes with police appeared to intensify in several cities in France, with the Lycée Nelson Mandela set on fire in Nantes and university students joining protests too. France’s prime minister called an inter-ministerial crisis meeting for early afternoon to address the protests. As President Emmanuel Macron’s government weighs up how to balance historic public debt with already strained state spending, an under-resourced and overstretched education sector is at the root of students’ anger. Students complain of teachers not being replaced when they leave and schools in a state of serious disrepair. High schools in poorer suburbs of cities across France have been at the center of the ongoing tensions with police. Toulouse, Nantes, Rennes, Lyon and Lille have all been host to violent confrontations between students and police, as well as arson on or near school property. Trash cans set alight In the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis, one of France’s most underprivileged areas and the epicenter of violence around Paris, video showed high schoolers setting fires outside the gates of the Lycée Paul Éluard, one of the focal points of violent protests, where students also tore down a section of fencing. Blockades were built and trash cans were set on fire outside a number of schools – a tactic common to major protests. “There are no windows, in the prefab toilets there’s no water, there are cockroaches and rats everywhere in the school. The school canteen is too expensive, there is no toilet paper in the toilets and we need to go and ask school supervisors to get some,” 17-year-old Fadila, a student at the Lycée Paul Éluard, which is currently undergoing renovations, told Reuters. “The buildings are dilapidated, in winter in the prefab classrooms it’s too cold, its -5 degrees Celsius (23 degrees Fahrenheit) and in the summer it’s 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit).” Some 400 schools have been affected nationwide by student blockades, backed in some institutions by teaching staff. Lawmakers from the far-left France Unbowed party turned up to support protests at numerous schools, including the mayor of Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko, who told journalists that “violence can be legitimate.” “Every time we can avoid it, it’s better,” he said, adding that young people should be held accountable for violating the law. But he continued: “They have the right to make a mistake.” “I understand the anxieties, sometimes the anger that our young people can have,” Macron told journalists during a state visit to Spain on Wednesday. “However, none of these fears, none of this debate, legitimizes violence. And in no case can those politically responsible (elected officials) – it’s a term that’s perhaps poorly chosen – legitimize violence. We’ve seen lots of politicians in front of schools drumming up students, I think that it’s serious.” Valérie Pécresse, president of the Île-de-France region, which surrounds and includes Paris, vowed in a post on X on Tuesday night to invoice Bagayoko for the 100,000-euro ($114,000) cost of repairing damage to the Lycée Paul Éluard. She estimated the cost of the protests in the region to total some 1 million euro. Pepper spray While Tuesday’s protest marches, led by unions, were largely peaceful, the police response to the protests at schools has been unforgiving, with video showing officers deploying pepper spray on adolescents as well as several instances of policeman aggressively tackling young protesters. Riot police were met with fireworks near the Lycée Paul Éluard on Tuesday, as anger spread at the police’s response. In one video shared on social media, a teenager was shot in the face with a tear-gas grenade at almost point-blank range by a policeman. A lawyer for family of the 14-year-old boy, identified as Eden L., accused the police of an “explosion of violence” and said that the family was submitting an official complaint to the police. CNN has reached out to the Saint-Denis police prefecture for comment. “We want fewer police because we feel there is an excessive amount of police repression, whether against high school student movements or social movements in general, most of which is completely unjustified,” student Mael Breton told Reuters on Tuesday. “We see this as a real problem, especially given the severe budget shortages elsewhere,” he said. On Thursday, France’s Education Minister Édouard Geffray promised on X to implement online learning for students affected by the disruption. “Violence will not deprive our students of their fundamental right to education,” he said.

articles.title: Flydubai attack gives Netanyahu new security message ahead of Israel vote
articles.summary: Motive behind Flydubai incident still unclear, but Israeli PM is framing it within his warnings of threats to Israelis.
articles.body:
Many questions about the apparent attempted hijacking of flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv remain unanswered. What was the motive of the attacker, the flight’s unnamed co-pilot , who stabbed the captain before being overpowered? What were the aims of his attack?

And yet, in contrast to the ambiguity that still exists, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – amidst his appearances greeting returning passengers – has been quick to frame the attack as the almost inevitable outcome of the “propaganda” he says continues to vilify Israel.

While conceding it was too early to establish a motive, Netanyahu nevertheless pointed to Iran – which Israel and the United States launched a war against in late February – and its proxies as intent on stepping up attacks on Israelis abroad. He claimed on Thursday that it had been established that the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination”.

For a politician who has long portrayed himself as the only leader capable of truly defending Israelis in the face of the threats he says they face, the attempted hijacking arguably bolsters Netanyahu’s narrative ahead of a pivotal parliamentary election later this month that will determine whether he remains Israel’s leader.

“It’s probably too early to say how this will pan out politically,” said former Israeli government adviser Daniel Levy, speaking to Al Jazeera.

“But it could have the advantage of removing many things that Netanyahu doesn’t want to see on the country’s front pages, such as the approaching anniversary of October 7 [2023 attacks on Israel], and replacing them with a story hinting at Iranian involvement, at the same time as other claims of possible Iranian operations are surfacing,” he said, referring to accusations of Tehran’s potential involvement in an incident near a US Air Force base in the United Kingdom.

“That would certainly give fresh impetus to the outcome that Netanyahu is pushing for – namely the resumption of intensified strikes against Iran, which also helps distract from Netanyahu’s domestic difficulties and could be touted as vindicating his warnings of earlier this week,” he said.

Netanyahu on Tuesday published a video statement in which he warned of “indications that, ahead of the elections, our enemies will try to attack us”, a warning his opponents swiftly dismissed as unevidenced fearmongering.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz, who called the plane attack an “attempted jihadist terror attack”, also appeared to refer back to the earlier warning, saying: “When the prime minister and I issue security warnings and alerts based on intelligence, everyone would do well, both our enemies abroad and uninformed former officials at home, to listen and take them seriously.”

However, Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid – who had received a security briefing from Netanyahu on Tuesday night – was quick to reject such a connection, saying on Wednesday that “nothing even resembling [the plane attack] appeared in the security briefing with the prime minister last night”.

For some observers who have followed Netanyahu – Israel’s longest-serving prime minister – for years, his actions following the attempted hijacking have been part of a long-running method of ensuring the aftermath of crises works in his favour.

“Netanyahu is trying to gain politically from the event,” said Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London. “You could see him, soon after the passengers landed in Israel, chatting with one of the Israeli heroes [who had subdued the co-pilot].”

But Bregman doesn’t necessarily think that Netanyahu, who polls predict may narrowly be beaten in the elections, will benefit.

“There is no political gain for him,” Bregman said. “[The attack] surprised him as it surprised all of us.”

Bregman added that Netanyahu’s only hope might be if a connection to Iran is established, leading to further escalation in the conflict with Tehran, which the US has appeared to be backing away from.

“There was clearly a security glitch which will be investigated,” Bregman told Al Jazeera. “It could have ended in another 9/11, but thanks to some brave passengers, and a massive amount of luck, it was averted.”

Speaking to US media on Wednesday, Netanyahu said that while it was “too early to say” who was behind the failed attempt to seize control of the plane, the co-pilot’s actions were the result of what he described as “fanaticism and hatred of an incalculable level”, sentiments that he suggested were tied to anti-Semitism because of international criticism of Israel.

Netanyahu’s claims of victimhood and persecution have ramped up in tandem with the rising tide of anger among many in the international community over Israel’s genocide in Gaza – in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians – its multiple strikes on neighbouring states, and widespread accusations of state complicity in the increasingly violent settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank, which has led numerous countries to impose restrictions on trade with Israel’s illegal settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory.

Addressing the sense of global outrage that he has since blamed for the attempted hijacking, Netanyahu told the United Nations General Assembly last month that Israel was fighting an “eighth front”, in addition to the seven fronts on which he said it was already fighting.

“It’s the war for truth. It is waged in the world’s media, and most perniciously, in social media,” he said, blaming the world’s media, including Al Jazeera, which sought to “brainwash young minds to hate Israel, hate America and hate the West”.

Al Jazeera Media Network has rejected Netanyahu’s attack, calling it the latest example of Israel’s “sustained campaign against Al Jazeera and its journalists”, which has resulted in the killing of 12 of its team in Gaza.

Israel’s government “will want to position the [attempted hijacking] attack against the backdrop of Netanyahu’s speech at the UN,” said Yossi Mekelberg, a senior consulting fellow at Chatham House.

“It just feeds into the sense of insecurity that many in Israel feel, as well as the trauma that has held since October 7,” he said, adding that it would also feed the sense of hypocrisy many in Israel feel at the sanctioning of a state for taking action against those it frames as intent on its destruction.

articles.title: Rick Ross charged with battery after alleged attack on girlfriend
articles.summary: Rapper Rick Ross was arrested Thursday after he was accused of beating his girlfriend at his Miami Beach home, according to authorities.
articles.body: Rapper Rick Ross was arrested Thursday after he was accused of beating his girlfriend at his Miami Beach home, according to authorities. Ross, whose legal name is William Leonard Roberts II, was charged with felony battery by strangulation and misdemeanor battery in connection with a domestic violence incident at his home on Miami Beach’s exclusive Star Island, according to a statement and affidavit from the Miami Beach Police Department. Police said the accuser reported that Ross, 50, struck her multiple times during an altercation on Aug. 28 and restricted her breathing by twisting the collar of her hoodie. The woman, whom police did not name, reported the incident to police on Tuesday. Ross turned himself in Thursday morning. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges. An attorney for Ross did not immediately return a request for comment. The woman provided detectives with a sworn statement and photographs documenting her injuries, police said. A criminal affidavit identifies the woman as Ross’ girlfriend at the time of the incident. On the morning of Aug. 28, Ross was “enraged” that his girlfriend was tagged in an Instagram photo, accused her of lying to him and slapped her across the face, the affidavit says. Later that morning, according to the police record, Ross accused her of having a romantic relationship with someone she said she was “merely friends with.” The woman told police that Ross then struck her in the chest several times and choked her “to the point she could not breathe by grabbing the collar of the hoodie she was wearing and twisting it,” the affidavit said. Ross then grabbed her by her ponytail and slammed her against a wall, the affidavit says. She told police she escaped the residence, returned and waited until Ross left before retrieving her belongings, according to the affidavit. The two dated for about a year, and lived together at the Star Island home at the time of the incident, the affidavit says. Ross is best known for his breakout single “Hustlin’,” released in 2006, as well as “Aston Martin Music” and “Stay Schemin.” He’s received nine Grammy nominations. The rapper’s bond was set at $5,000 for the battery by strangulation charge and $1,000 for the battery charge, according to online jail records. “I’m totally innocent of these fabricated allegations made against me,” Ross said, leaving the jailhouse “I repeat: I’m totally innocent of these fabricated allegations made against me.” Ross said he would be traveling to Dubai on Friday and in Paris on Saturday. If you or someone you know is facing domestic violence, call the National Domestic Violence hotline for help at (800) 799-SAFE (7233), or go to for more. States often have domestic violence hotlines as well.

articles.title: ‘Tea With Omar’: College Student Finds Comfort in Tea Ceremonies. Here Are Tips for the Perfect Cup
articles.summary: Omar Hernandez-Tena, who goes by “Tea With Omar” on TikTok, is a Brown University junior who loves Chinese tea culture, particularly gongfu cha (tea with skill).
articles.body: A Brown University junior has become one of the internet’s most beloved tea enthusiasts. Omar Hernandez-Tena, who goes by the moniker “Tea With Omar” on TikTok, studies electrical engineering at Brown and loves Chinese tea culture, particularly gongfu cha (tea with skill). Since midsummer, he’s been sharing his love almost every day with his followers. The 20-year-old starts nearly every video with a cheerful greeting — “Hi, everyone!” — then shows off the day’s tea selection. In a Sept. 20 video, it’s white moonlight tea, also known as Yue Guang Bai. He explains some of the tea’s attributes, including its “hairy” nature and fresh scent, with notes of grapes and lilac. With every sip he takes, you can see his stress melt away — and he passes the this feeling of calm on to the viewer. Hernandez-Tena typically shows the full, unedited tea-brewing process, from heating his cháhú (teapot) with hot water to pouring his first brew into his chápán (tea tray) and feeding his tea pet with leftover or rinse tea. “I started getting into this specific tea consumption method probably earlier this year,” Hernandez-Tena tells TODAY.com. “But in general, I’ve been drinking tea a long time.” And the student’s fanbase is growing steadily: He only started posting about his love of tea on July 30 and already boasts more than 172,000 followers. His fans appreciate his calming demeanor, with one commenting that he brings “peace into my life, like genuinely.” Hernandez-Tena says his online tea practice is getting him recognized on campus, which he calls “shocking,” but he’s trying to keep his priorities in check. “I call my dad a lot because my family’s been quite supportive,” he says. “He always reminds me that school is the most important thing, because at the end of the day, I’m here to get my college degree.” Tea With Omar’s Brewing Tips Hernandez-Tena has tips for those trying to get into their own tea practice: Small Businesses Over Big Stores “In general, I’m very pro-small business,” he says, adding that there are a lot of small tea businesses on the internet, but brick-and-mortar stores are the way to go. “In general, if you want something in person, I feel like that’s the best thing,” he says. “Just look up ‘loose-leaf tea stores near me.’” Tea Temperatures “It varies for all,” he says. Hernandez-Tena says to use the right temperature for the tea you have: Oolong tea needs a much lower temperature than black teas, which require boiling water to brew. Steep Your Tea Correctly Hernandez-Tena says it’s important to use the correct ratio of water to leaves, even if you’re just using a mug. “My general ratio for three grams of tea is eight ounces of water,” he says for loose-leaf tea. “That matters, because if you use too much water, it’s gonna taste not strong.” He also suggests brewing for at least three minutes. Not All Matcha Is Created Equal Hernandez-Tena often shares his love of matcha and suggests going into the store already knowing what you want. “They all say they’re ‘ceremonial grade,’ but that doesn’t really hold much value on the Japanese market,” he says. He suggests looking for a blend of first-harvest and second-harvest leaves in your matcha powder, as first-harvest-only powders can get pricey. “First-harvest leaves are the best ones because they took their time to grow, and they’re very complex and beautiful and delicate,” he says. “If you’re really fancy and you really want to get the best stuff, that’s when you would start looking into whether your matcha is single cultivar or not.” Fruity Chinese Teas Exist If you aren’t into floral or earthy flavors, Hernandez-Tena says many Chinese teas have more fruity notes you can try, from the peachy Da Hong Pao to the figgy Jing Jun Mei to white peony teas, which he says “tastes like grape” if you brew them correctly. Be Present — and Maybe Get a Tea Tray “I’m very active in this ceremony,” Hernandez-Tena says, pouring hot water over his lime-lemon tea pet. “The tea smells amazing, the tea tastes amazing and, actually, I love hearing the water move around the tea table,” he adds. “It’s reminding me a lot of the beauty of life and the little things we should really appreciate.” Tea Ceremonies Can Help With Mental Health “It’s really good for mental health,” he says. “There’s a lot of intention that I put into it when I do this, and it’s really good for my brain to just be engaged at that time.” “You know, sometimes I’m in the library all day doing random problem sets, and my brain reaches a point where I’m numb,” he adds. “But with tea, there’s no technology. There’s no physics. There’s no electrical engineering involved. It’s just me, the tea and my thoughts.”

articles.title: Hezbollah received $157M in weapons in 2024, mostly from 1 nation, report says
articles.summary: The Israeli Center for Research of Terror Financing found Iran gave Hezbollah $129 million in rockets, missiles, drones and anti-tank missiles in 2024.
articles.body: Hezbollah terrorists in Yemen received $157 million worth of weapons in 2024, most of it given freely by Iran, according to a new report from the Israeli nonprofit Center for Research of Terror Financing (CENTEF). The report, titled "Hezbollah Financial Statements," relied on open-source data as well as known valuations of Hezbollah's military assets, according to the Jerusalem Post. The report found that Hezbollah spent just $28 million on procuring weapons, and those were limited to small arms, ammunition, drone components, dual-use equipment and equipment obtained through its international procurement networks. EXCLUSIVE: ISRAEL SEIZES VAST IRAN TERROR AXIS ARSENAL WITH SURPRISING FOREIGN ORIGINS Meanwhile, CENTEF said Iran provided roughly $129 million worth of weapons as an in-kind grant, including rockets, missiles, drones, ATGMs, air-defense systems, ammunition, launchers, naval equipment and IED-related assets. The CENTEF analysis found that Hezbollah acquired 4,000 short-range Katyusha rockets, 400 Falaq-1 and 2 rockets, and 120 Burkan rockets in 2024. The short-range rockets are estimated to cost $300 per unit, while the Burkan rockets are estimated to cost $400. IDF UNCOVERS HEZBOLLAH WEAPONS STASH INSIDE HOSPITAL IN LEBANON The report also detailed more sophisticated weaponry obtained by Hezbollah, including Iran’s Fajr series and Syrian-origin heavy rockets. The Fajr-3 is a 240mm artillery rocket armed with a 45-kilogram warhead, while the Fajr-5 is a 333mm rocket with a GPS-guided Fajr-5C variant, according to the Post. The rockets are estimated to cost $2,000 to $10,000, and CENTEF estimates Hezbollah obtained 600 of them in 2024. HEZBOLLAH'S 'GAME CHANGING' NIGHT-HUNTING WEAPON PUNCHES THROUGH ISRAEL'S DEFENSES: EXPERT Anti-tank guided missiles make up a major portion of Hezbollah's arsenal. The research found that the Russian-made Kornet and Iran's reverse-engineered Dehlavieh make up the bulk of Hezbollah's ATGMs, with the former costing approximately $26,000 per round and the latter costing an estimated $12,000 to $15,000, according to the Post. Hezbollah has expended vast measures of its arsenal in its attacks against Israel over the past year, and Israeli forces have decimated the group's leadership ranks. Sarit Zehavi, the founder and president of the Israel-based Alma Research and Education Center, told Fox News Digital earlier this month that the IDF has decimated 90% of Hezbollah’s rocket and missile arsenal. Most of the array of sophisticated missiles, accurate missiles and long-range missiles was either eliminated or neutralized," Zehavi said. Fox News' Benjamin Weinthal contributed to this report.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Trump’s new security alliance faces first real-world test deep in South America as troops deploy
articles.summary: Donald Trump's Shield of the Americas faces its first real test as Bolivia deploys forces to strategic routes amid renewed blockade and unrest fears.
articles.body: Bolivia’s mounting security challenge is emerging as one of the first real-world tests of President Donald Trump’s Shield of the Americas, the country’s defense minister told Fox News Digital, as security forces deploy to strategic locations and the government braces for renewed unrest. "I believe this is one of the first real tests of whether Shield of the Americas can move from declarations to concrete results," Bolivian Defense Minister Ernesto Justiniano told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview. But Justiniano stressed that Bolivia is not declaring that a coup attempt is underway. "I am not saying today that we have proven evidence of a specific operation currently underway to overthrow the President," he said. "What we do have are very serious precedents and warning signs that justify preventive action." Trump launched Shield of the Americas at a March summit in Florida, bringing together governments across the Western Hemisphere to deepen economic and security cooperation, including efforts to combat transnational crime. TRUMP ADMIN BACKS BOLIVIA STATE OF EMERGENCY AS LEFTIST EX-LEADER'S LOYALISTS FRACTURE NATION Justiniano's comments come as President Rodrigo Paz’s government attempts to prevent a repeat of more than 50 days of road blockades earlier this year that caused shortages of food, fuel and medicine and deepened the country’s economic crisis. On Sept. 17, Bolivia’s Assembly approved a 90-day extension of the country’s state of emergency, citing persistent risks of renewed blockades. Some opposition lawmakers and social groups criticized the measure, arguing that it failed to address the underlying causes of the unrest. Reuters A U.S. official told Fox News Digital that, "The United States is unwavering in its commitment to support Bolivia’s democracy and the Paz Administration as it rebuilds the country after 20 years of failed socialist policies. The Trump Administration will continue to stand with Bolivia as it works toward stability, security, and a better future for all Bolivians." "The threat is serious enough for us to take preventive measures, but I do not want to portray a government that is under siege or weak," Justiniano said. "There is one fundamental difference: Bolivia learned… We do not confuse legitimate social discontent with a threat to democracy. People may agree or disagree with our economic policies. They can march, protest and challenge the government. That is democracy. What is not democratic is trying to impose a decision through violence, indefinite blockades or threats against the constitutional order." The defense minister confirmed that police and military forces have already been deployed preventively around the country. ‘WAVE OF FREEDOM’ SWEEPS LATIN AMERICA AS TRUMP ALLY TAKES FIGHT TO MARXIST TERROR GROUP "There is a preventive deployment in different parts of the country, particularly along strategic routes, access points to major cities and locations considered sensitive for freedom of movement, supply lines and the protection of critical infrastructure," Justiniano said. He declined to provide exact locations, troop numbers or unit movements, saying the scale of the deployment would change according to the level of risk. The unfolding situation comes just days after Trump hosted leaders participating in Shield of the Americas on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Sept. 22. The White House has described the initiative as an alliance focused on economic and national security in the Western Hemisphere. The White House PRESIDENT PAZ: BOLIVIA HAS REJECTED SOCIALISM AND IS OPEN FOR BUSINESS A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital that "the United States values its close partnership with Bolivia, a Shield of the Americas participant, to advance economic growth and solve the security challenges posed by corruption and transnational crime." "President Paz survived 53 days of blockades and violent attempts to undermine his presidency," the spokesperson said. "As the country’s elected leader, we support his administration’s ongoing work to repair Bolivia’s economy after more than 20 years of corrupt mismanagement by Evo Morales’s Movement towards Socialism (MAS) party." The State Department also said visa restrictions announced Sept. 28 targeted Bolivian nationals whom Washington says are undermining "the security and governance progress President Paz and his administration are achieving," adding that the actions "reinforce, not undercut, our cooperation." The Trump administration revoked visas for 27 officials, former officials and relatives across Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, according to the Associated Press. Among those affected was Bolivian Prosecutor General Roger Mariaca, whom the State Department accused of corruption and facilitating narcotrafficking. Mariaca has rejected the allegations. Justiniano said Bolivia has formally requested the information underlying the U.S. action. "The case of Bolivia’s Prosecutor General, Roger Mariaca, is particularly serious because the U.S. government has publicly made specific allegations involving corruption and the facilitation of drug trafficking," he said. But the defense minister cautioned against drawing a direct connection between those affected by the visa restrictions and the current unrest. "It would be irresponsible for me to automatically state that everyone affected by those measures is connected to the current mobilizations," Justiniano said. "We do not have public evidence that would justify that generalization." Asked what assistance Washington is providing in response to the current threat, Justiniano declined to say whether the U.S. was supplying operational intelligence or other direct assistance. EXCLUSIVE: FBI EXTRADITIONS SOAR AS PATEL RAMPS UP FOREIGN OUTREACH, VOWS 'NO SANCTUARY' "What I can say is that Bolivia wants to deepen this cooperation," he said. Justiniano said Bolivia is seeking closer cooperation with the United States on information sharing, financial intelligence, counter-narcotics, organized crime, border security, extraditions, training and institutional strengthening. That push was already evident last week, when Bolivian Minister of the Presidency Fernando Aramayo told Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly that the Paz government views its struggle against organized crime as part of a wider regional challenge. "We recognize the legitimacy of protests and demonstrations that demand responses from the government," Aramayo said. "What we are attacking right now is all the attacks against our democracy that have been financed by narco-traffic money and organized international crime." Aramayo said the government had received support from Washington. "The White House has supported us and other countries in this fight against these dark forces," he said, adding that Bolivia was "very proud of being part of this mechanism like the Shield of Americas." Asked whether state actors were also involved in fueling the unrest, Aramayo said corruption and organized crime had become deeply embedded during the previous two decades, claiming that institutions, social and political leaders and private-sector actors had become entangled with transnational criminal organizations. Justiniano stressed that the military deployments are not intended to suppress peaceful demonstrations and said police retain primary responsibility for public order. "We are preparing for a risk, not declaring that a coup is underway," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The distinction goes to the heart of the challenge confronting Shield of the Americas: how a regional initiative built in part to combat cartels and transnational organized crime operates when a member government says those networks are intersecting with domestic political unrest.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: BAPS France on Thursday welcomed the findings of an investigation that found no explicit request from the religious group to remove or exclude
articles.body: NEW DELHI: BAPS France on Thursday welcomed the findings of an investigation that found no explicit request from the religious group to remove or exclude female staff during its delegation’s visit to the Eiffel Tower.In a statement, BAPS France reiterated that it had never asked for female employees to be hidden, removed or excluded from the visit.“Following the publication of the official investigation findings concerning our delegation's visit to the Eiffel Tower, BAPS wishes first to reiterate its concern for the employees affected by the events surrounding the visit,” it said.“From the outset, BAPS has consistently stated that it never asked for female employees to be hidden, removed or excluded. The investigation establishes this fact that BAPS made no such request for women to be excluded along the visitor route. We hope this clarification will contribute to a better understanding of the circumstances and allow everyone involved to move forward respectfully,” it added.The statement comes days after female employees at the Eiffel Tower alleged that they were excluded during a private visit by a BAPS delegation. The allegations led staff to go on strike, following which the Eiffel Tower was closed for a day.What the probe foundAn investigation by the General Inspectorate of the City of Paris found that there had been “no explicit request” from BAPS regarding the removal of female staff.“The initial request brought to the attention of SETE concerned the lack of physical contact between religious figures and women,” the investigation report said.According to the report, employees working at the reception and in customer relations were asked to temporarily leave “during the ascent of part of the delegation to the North pillar”.A cleaning service provider’s employee was then asked to wait until her break, while another female employee was replaced in an elevator during the group’s descent. These actions eventually resulted in female staff being sidelined, according to the report accessed by Le Parisien.The City of Paris’s Inspector General attributed the incident to “an internal process in which a requirement for no contact was progressively translated into the assignment of male staff to various positions, and then extended in its implementation to the point of dismissing or replacing female employees already in place”.“Through word of mouth, the message was distorted,” the probe found.Eiffel Tower chief to step downMeanwhile, the operating firm that runs the Eiffel Tower confirmed that its director general, Patrick Branco Ruivo, will step down by the end of the year.Société d’Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE) said Ruivo would leave his post after an internal investigation found that “operational flaws and shortcomings” in the organisation of the visit had led to female staff being removed from their positions, AFP reported.SETE said in a statement that the failures resulted “in female staff being excluded from the visit that day, an unacceptable situation”.You use AI every day. articles.title: Judge ends case against Olympian accused of Reflecting Pool vandalism
articles.summary: Judge said Trump might target champion canoeist because he was politically active and donated to Democrats.
articles.body:
A judge in Washington DC has dismissed the criminal case against an Olympian accused by the Trump administration of vandalising the Reflecting Pool.

Judge Todd Edelman ordered the case against David Hearn dismissed "with prejudice", meaning US prosecutors cannot refile the case.

The US Justice Department had dropped the case after new evidence emerged, but Hearn's lawyers expressed concern that US President Donald Trump could pressure prosecutors to revive it.

Issues with the pool were the result of a "rushed and botched" job by contractors, the government found, but Trump has repeatedly claimed it was due to vandalism and urged prosecutors to target Hearn, citing donations to Democrats.

The cases against three other people also accused of vandalising the pool were dropped as well, but Hearn's defence attorneys said they were worried he would be specifically targeted by Trump because he is a politically active person who previously made campaign donations to Democrats.

In permanently dismissing the case, Edelman agreed with those concerns and pointed to public statements made by Trump after his chief prosecutor for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro, dropped the case.

"Although the prosecutors assigned to this case have deemed it meritless, the president of the United States has repeatedly disparaged them and pressured them to change course," the judge said in his order, published on Thursday.

"Mr Hearn faces the unique possibility that the government will revive this case – one that it has already announced to be meritless – based on political pressure brought by the president of the United States upon his subordinate officers."

Hearn, a champion canoeist, had been facing a 10-year prison sentence if he had been found guilty. He previously told the BBC that he was riding his bike near the pool when he reached down to touch a piece of the lining that was peeling.

The Justice Department said new information from the Department of Interior (DOI) indicated "that damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in June 2026 was the result of flawed installation by the contractor" and "the rush to complete the project prior to events associated with the America 250 celebration in the weeks surrounding Independence Day 2026".

The concession represented a stunning about-face for prosecutors who had just days before accused Hearn of "a deliberate act to damage the Reflecting Pool".

Trump then took to social media to say he disagreed "100%" with Pirro's decision to drop the charges, describing it in separate statements as "a disgrace" and "stupid".

"There may have been some contractor difficulty, but the major damage was caused by VANDALS!" the president wrote in August. Trump has urged Pirro to revive the case against Hearn.

"US Attorney Jeanine Pirro should re-visit her hastily made decision, especially since it turned out that the 'gentleman' involved is a big player in ActBlue," he said on 7 August, referring to Hearn and the campaign fundraising platform used by Democrats.

He also disparaged Norm Eisen, one of the attorneys representing Hearn, who previously worked for President Barack Obama, as well as on an impeachment case against Trump during his first term.

Hearn's legal team hailed the permanent dismissal as "a victory for the rule of law".

"This administration chose to pursue an unjust prosecution against Mr. Hearn. It should not get repeated chances to wield the power of criminal prosecution against someone who should never have been prosecuted," they said. "Today's decision protects Mr. Hearn from that threat, allowing him to move forward with his life as he deserves."

Asked for comment about the decision, a White House spokesperson referred the BBC to Trump's online comments which were cited by the judge, including his suggestion the case should not have been dropped. The BBC has also contacted Pirro's office and the justice department for comment.

Trump administration drops Reflecting Pool vandalism charge and admits 'botched' repairs

The Lincoln Memorial and the adjoining Reflecting Pool have been the site of many landmark events including civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr's famous "I have a dream" speech.

It underwent a multi-million dollar resealing and painting project this spring, one of several construction efforts in the US capital personally directed by Trump.

The monument had long been beset by structural failures and leaks, and Trump championed the project as part of his bid to beautify the capital city.

But, despite the makeover, which cost an estimated $16m (£12m), the pool continued to be plagued by algae, while pieces of the blue sealant peeled off days after it was applied.

articles.title: Photos: Palestinians mourn more than 100 loved ones in mass Gaza funeral
articles.summary: The remains of 105 people were buried in the Sheikh Radwan cemetery, northwest of Gaza City.
articles.body:
Palestinians have buried the remains of 105 people killed in a series of Israeli air strikes nearly three years ago.

The strikes involved at least 20 bombs that levelled the seven-storey Al Taj 3 building and destroyed several other residential buildings in the Yarmouk Square neighbourhood of Gaza City on the afternoon of October 25, 2023.

The remains of those killed were carried in a large funeral procession on Thursday and buried in the Sheikh Radwan cemetery, northwest of Gaza City.

Civil defence operations director Abdul al-Majdalawi said it had been “impossible” to reach the bodies at the time of the attack.

The recovery operation was the fifth largest of its kind since Israel launched its genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza in October 2023, in terms of the number of bodies recovered, said Al Jazeera correspondent Ibrahim al-Khalili, reporting from Gaza City.

articles.title: France rocked by student riots as hundreds arrested, violence spreads nationwide
articles.summary: Violent student protests continue to spread across France, with school blockades, clashes with police and officials warning of outside agitators.
articles.body: More than 625 people, mostly students, have been arrested over two days of violent protests near schools and universities across France over what students say are staffing shortages, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded classes, government budget cuts and long schedules. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu convened a crisis meeting Thursday, canceling ministers’ trips to focus on the protests, which began last week in Paris-region schools and have snowballed. EUROPE’S LEFT COURTS MUSLIM VOTERS AS ANTI-ISRAEL POLITICS RESHAPE CONTINENT Reports say over 350 high schools and about 30 university campuses were affected by the movement on Thursday alone. RFI reported 83 police and gendarmes were wounded today, with 119 students and school staffers injured since the start of unrest last week. Reuters reported the principal of Marseille’s Victor Hugo high school was doused in gasoline and injured, while two other principals were injured in attacks in Rouen and Petit-Quevilly. Police used tear gas in several cities, with Reuters reporting students accusing authorities of heavy‑handed tactics. Meanwhile, authorities are warning of "urban violence" and attempted arson at multiple schools. The protests coincide with the government announcing a series of unpopular spending cuts in its 2027 budget two weeks ago and have become a political flashpoint at a ​sensitive moment for the French government. GLOBAL RISE IN ANTISEMITISM LEAVES JEWISH COMMUNITY ISOLATED; RABBI SAYS WORLD AT 'A TIPPING POINT' Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told Reuters that, "in certain places, there were individuals acting as agitators — people who moved from one school to another to stir up high school and other students and incite them to commit acts of violence." Education Minister Edouard Geffray called for schools to hold classes remotely if protesters were blocking their premises, posting on X: "Violence will not keep our students from their fundamental right to ​an education." Senior Envoy to Europe at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies Simone Rodan-Benzaquen told Fox News Digital, "The students’ grievances about missing teachers and deteriorating schools were real at first. But dousing a principal in gasoline and attacking firefighters are acts of extreme violence. What makes this politically significant is the effort to turn frustration over schools into a much broader confrontation with the government." The Associated Press reported the protests are quickly blowing up as a hot topic in the election campaign to replace President Emmanuel Macron next May. Far-left presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon has decried the government response to the protests as repressive. Critics have accused his party, La France Insoumise, (LFI), of seeking to use the unrest to score points in the presidential campaign and of inciting violence. GERMAN OFFICIALS WARN ISLAMIST, FAR-LEFT RHETORIC DRIVING SPIKE IN ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS Rodan-Benzaquen says the LFI has "actively supported the mobilization. Activists circulate footage of clashes, party accounts amplify it and elected officials present themselves as the students’ defenders." With an election next year, she said, "Mélenchon sees these mobilizations as a way to consolidate young voters and marginalize the moderate left. At a time of deep political, geopolitical and economic challenges, this is a very dangerous situation for France." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Video posted to social media shows the Seine-Saint Denis mayor, Bally Bagayoko of the LFI, joining in with students, smiling and high-fiving pupils after a trash can was set on fire in the street. And the president of the Île‑de‑France region told Radio Monte Carlo, "There is a call to action being issued by LFI today: ‘Trash your high school.’ It is being spread via TikTok challenges." In Madrid on Wednesday, Macron told reporters, "High schools are meant to be open and to share knowledge. They are not meant to be blockaded or to have trash cans set on fire." The Associated Press, Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Iran's 'village' is cracking. How Tehran is keeping its Axis of Resistance alive
articles.summary: Mothers and the Islamic Republic of Iran have something unexpected in common: they both understand that it takes a village to raise a child, though what a
articles.body: Mothers and the Islamic Republic of Iran have something unexpected in common: they both understand that it takes a village to raise a child, though what a child and a village mean to each of them differs.For Iran, the child is its influence in the Middle East and its village, the network it has built over the years in this same region –– Hezbollah in Lebanon, militias in Iraq, the Houthis in Yemen and armed groups elsewhere, each with its own capabilities, interests and relationship with Tehran.The groups operate in very different political and military environments, but together they give Iran a way to contest its adversaries without committing its own forces to every battlefield.But the village is not as strong as it once was, and the recent conflict has shown where its foundations have cracked or given way.How Tehran keeps it standing comes down to four moves: pacing its partners, replacing the ones it has lost, paying for all of it through channels that sanctions have made costlier without closing, and tolerating allies it cannot command.Iran's villageThe Axis of Resistance exists because of fear. On January 29, 2002, George W Bush put Iran, Iraq and North Korea in his "Axis of Evil", at a moment when the United States had already invaded Afghanistan and was preparing for war in Iraq. American power was closing in on Iran from two sides, and Tehran had reason to believe it could be next.The habit of reaching beyond its borders was by then two decades old. Iran had sent Revolutionary Guards to Lebanon in 1982 to train the Shia fighters who would form Hezbollah, and during the Iran-Iraq war it had organised Iraqi Shia exiles into the force that became the Badr Organization. The speech and the wars that followed turned that habit into a doctrine of strategic depth, in which armed partners in different theatres would force Iran's opponents to account for several fronts at once and keep a confrontation from reaching Iranian territory first.The network was never uniform. Hezbollah became deeply integrated with Tehran, Iraqi militias developed their own political bases, and the Houthis kept far greater autonomy. That unevenness decides what Tehran can ask of each member.The strainSince the war began on 28 February, the arrangement has been tested harder than at any point in its history. Hezbollah has been badly weakened, Syria's role as the land bridge to Lebanon ended with the fall of Assad, and Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei has been killed. A ceasefire and a memorandum of understanding followed in June, then came apart over the Strait of Hormuz.Manish Rai, a geopolitical analyst specialising in the Middle East and Af-Pak region, traces the breakdown to one clause. "The strikes were resumed because of the different interpretations of article 5 in MoU which concerns the Strait of Hormuz," he says. Washington wants the strait kept as it was before 28 February, while Iran, which had begun fining vessels for transiting it, wants control. American forces began nightly strikes on 11 July, and diplomacy has since stalled: by the war's seventh month Trump had rejected an Iranian offer of a seven-day ceasefire, and the Wall Street Journal reported that he expects the bombing to resume after the November midterms.Pace the partnersRai also points out that Tehran has not been to throw everything into the fight at once. To maintain their control the leadership, he says, advised its partners to pursue low-intensity conflict, since an all-out war could destroy groups such as Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad while a slower campaign still drains an adversary. Some groups were held back, among them Bahrain's Al-Ashtar Brigade and the Shia units of Pakistan and Afghanistan, which have gone into what he calls "a bit of hibernation" because Tehran has no wish to open fronts against Islamabad or Kabul.The logic behind their strategy is endurance. Tehran does not need every partner to fight at full strength, or even to enter the war at the same time. It needs enough of them to remain intact, armed and capable of being activated when circumstances demand it. A slower, uneven campaign allows Iran to keep pressure on its adversaries while limiting the risk of exhausting the very groups it may need in a later phase. In that sense, the network is not built for one decisive battle; it is built to absorb losses, preserve its remaining capabilities and keep multiple fronts available for as long as the conflict lasts.Replace what has been lostHezbollah is the most capable member of the Axis, and Rai argues that if Israel reduces it to a shadow of its former self, the resulting void "cannot be filled by any other Iranian-supported organisations".Diplomacy is working against it as well as force. A US-brokered framework signed on 26 June ties a phased Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon to the disarmament of non-state armed groups, a reference to Hezbollah, which rejected the terms and insists that withdrawal come first. That dispute over sequencing has outlasted several rounds of talks, while Israeli strikes in the south continue.What Tehran can do is shift weight to the partners it still reaches. Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces are the obvious candidate, because they are next door and large, an estimated 100,000 to 125,000 fighters by Rai's count, with Kataib Hezbollah and the Badr Organization among them.He describes them as Tehran's "personal favourites", available as ground forces for the Revolutionary Guards and as an internal-security backstop that would free elite Iranian units for operations against the United States and Israel.Substitution also has a limit, Hezbollah has built loyalty over decades through its social services, and as Rai suggests, "if the US, Israel, and international organisations such as the United Nations provide sufficient funding for these services, public support could gradually shift from Hezbollah to the Lebanese state."An army can be replaced faster than a constituency, and that is as true in Beirut as in Tehran's calculations.Keep the money movingAll of this has to be paid for, but Iran's financial support for its partners does not move through one pipeline. It runs through a mix of sanctioned oil sales, front companies, informal banking networks, cash, trade intermediaries and, increasingly, digital assets. The system is designed less to make money invisible than to make it difficult for any single disruption to stop the flow altogether.American sanctions this year have targeted several parts of that machinery. In April, Washington moved against an oil-for-gold network that it said generated revenue for Hezbollah and the Quds Force. In July, the US Treasury targeted a maritime-services network linked to Iran that it said used digital assets to facilitate payments, while continuing to sanction vessels involved in the country's shadow-fleet trade. Earlier sanctions have also identified front companies and intermediaries operating outside Iran, including in Hong Kong and the Gulf.Rai describes a parallel informal system in which sanctioned crude is sold through shadow tankers, proceeds are moved through front companies and intermediaries, and hawala networks settle payments across borders without relying on conventional banks. Some money can move as cash, while other transfers can be disguised through commercial transactions, charities or businesses that have legitimate operations alongside their financial role. Cryptocurrency provides another route where conventional banking channels are difficult or unavailable.But the financial relationship between Tehran and its partners is not simply one-way. Hezbollah, the Houthis and other groups have developed their own revenue streams, from businesses and investments to taxation, smuggling and other illicit activity, reducing their dependence on Iranian transfers. That distinction matters because sanctions can make Iranian support more expensive and complicated without necessarily making the organisations themselves financially helpless.The result is a system that is under pressure but difficult to shut down. Every new sanctions round can force Tehran and its partners to change intermediaries, routes or payment methods, but the network has accumulated enough alternative channels to keep at least some money moving. For Iran, financial resilience is therefore less about maintaining an uninterrupted flow than about ensuring that when one channel closes, another remains available.Tolerate allies it cannot commandThe Houthis show where this strategy runs out. Ansar Allah began in the early 1990s as a nationalist and cultural movement against Salafi influence and the marginalisation of Yemen's Zaydis, and drew close to Tehran only after turning sectarian. It does not accept velayat-e faqih, the doctrine of clerical guardianship that Hezbollah and many Iraqi militias follow, and its first aim is power at home. Rai calls it "an independent ally, rather than a strict proxy".The summer tested that, the Houthis stayed out of the Saudi front until 13 July, when Saudi Arabia struck Sanaa airport to stop an Iranian plane returning their delegation from Khamenei's funeral. They responded with missiles at a southern Saudi airport, then declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia and hit two major Saudi oil facilities on the Red Sea, and on 8 September a barrage wounded seventy-three people in the kingdom.The Houthis escalated only after an affront to their own delegation, which suits a cautious, self-interested actor, yet their targets are the ones that most relieve pressure on Iran, and Rai says Tehran has encouraged threats against Bab el-Mandeb and the East-West "Petroline" pipeline built to bypass Hormuz.Yemen's war has its own logic too, since government forces say their offensive aims at retaking Sanaa. Tehran can decide when to activate an ally and cannot necessarily dictate how it fights, which is the cost of an Axis that keeps going partly because its members do not wait for orders.Iran gains from Saudi Arabia's predicament, since Riyadh has avoided direct retaliation against Iran, calling the war "not our war", and has refused the US Navy the use of its bases for the Hormuz navigation effort. Rai says it fears offending religious sentiment at home and forfeiting its standing as leader of the Sunni world, while the United Arab Emirates has taken a harder line by cooperating with Israel and striking inside Iran. A divided Gulf suits a strategy of attrition, though Houthi and Iraqi pressure may be pushing Riyadh towards limited retaliation.The test in IraqIraq is where the four moves now face their clearest test. On September 30, the United States completed its military withdrawal from Iraq, formally ending the Operation Inherent Resolve mission after more than a decade. Washington will continue to support Baghdad with training and intelligence, but the security responsibility now rests with the Iraqi state.The other deadline did not end with the American departure. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had originally tied the disarmament of armed factions to September 30, but Baghdad has since pushed the deadline to June 30, 2027. Under the revised plan, Iran-aligned armed groups are expected to observe a 90-day halt to attacks before beginning a gradual handover of weapons to the state. The timetable is already facing resistance: some of the most powerful factions have rejected the idea of surrendering their weapons voluntarily.That makes the American withdrawal less a conclusion than the beginning of a new test. For years, the presence of US forces gave Iran-backed groups both a target and a justification for maintaining an armed role. With those forces gone, Baghdad has less room to argue that the militias are needed to resist a foreign military presence, but it also has to prove that the state can enforce its authority without triggering a confrontation with the factions themselves.If Baghdad succeeds, Iran's village loses one of its most important advantages: an armed network embedded inside a partner state. If it fails, the American withdrawal may leave the militias with greater room to operate, even as Baghdad formally insists that all weapons must come under state authority.The village has survived by bending: it has paced its partners, shifted weight to those closest to home, found money through channels that pressure has narrowed without closing, and put up with allies who answer to their own politics. The same flexibility that has kept it standing is also what Tehran can no longer fully control.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Record electric rate goes into effect in Puerto Rico amid soaring costs, demands
articles.summary: The new rate which far surpasses the average rate for residential customers in the U.S. mainland, is expected to drive up an already high cost of living in the U.S. territory.
articles.body: SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico — A record electric rate went into effect Thursday in Puerto Rico as outages persist and the U.S. territory’s power grid continues to crumble. A residential customer that consumes 800 kilowatt-hours a month will see the monthly bill rise about 18%, from $229 to $271, according to Puerto Rico’s Energy Bureau, which approved the increase. The new rate will remain in effect until at least Dec. 31 and is expected to drive up an already high cost of living on the island of 3.2 million people, where more than 40% of residents live in poverty. The new rate of 33.86 cents per kWh far surpasses the average rate of 18.3 cents per kWh for residential customers in the U.S. mainland, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Luma Energy, which oversees the transmission and distribution of power in Puerto Rico, had requested an increase of more than six cents per kWh and stressed that it would not generate additional revenue for the company, but rather cover an increase in costs. “The difference is driven by higher energy consumption due to high summer temperatures, rising global oil prices resulting from the conflict in the Middle East — which has constrained fuel transportation and increased costs — greater use of customer batteries, and the need to rely on more expensive fuel when power plants do not generate enough electricity,” Luma said in a statement. The increase comes as outages persist nearly a decade after Puerto Rico’s power grid was razed by Hurricane Maria when it struck the island in 2017 as a powerful Category 4 storm, although the grid was already weak given a lack of maintenance and investment for decades. Last week, a large fire that erupted at a substation left more than 200,000 customers without power in the latest outage to hit the island. The Energy Bureau said in a statement late Wednesday that it approved an increase of 5.28 cents per kWh to reduce the financial burden on customers. It noted that it did not pass along the cost of $17.6 million associated with what it called alleged failures by New Fortress Energy to supply fuel from June to August. “Fuel costs must not be automatically passed on to the consumer simply because they were incurred or billed,” the Energy Bureau said. New Fortress Energy supplies natural gas to power generation plants on Puerto Rico’s north coast. Currently, those plants are using diesel — driving up costs — because a vessel laden with a delivery of natural gas has been blocked from entering the San Juan Bay for two weeks given its size. The case remains mired in court. The Energy Bureau said it also is investigating some $19 million that Luma said was paid for gas quantities that officials say exceeded what Genera PR “ultimately needed or could receive.” Genera PR oversees the generation of power in Puerto Rico. The increase comes as the administration of Puerto Rico Gov. Jenniffer González pushes to cancel the contract with Luma, with the case currently tied up in court with ongoing lawsuits. Luma and Genera PR were awarded contracts as Puerto Rico’s state-owned Electric Power Authority struggles to restructure its more than $9 billion debt load. In 2024, petroleum represented 63% of the island’s overall energy use; natural gas accounted for 31%, coal 5% and renewables 1%, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

articles.title: Renee Good’s family sues Trump administration over fatal ICE shooting
articles.summary: Lawsuits accuse Trump officials of recklessness and civil rights violations in Renee Good’s fatal Minneapolis shooting .
articles.body:
The family of Renee Good, one of two US citizens fatally shot by federal immigration agents in the state of Minnesota, has sued the government over her killing during a sweeping immigrant deportation blitz in January.

The two lawsuits – filed on Thursday by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and Renee’s brother, Brent Ganger – say officials from US President Donald Trump’s administration were reckless and violated the civil rights of Good and others in Minneapolis. The lawsuits are demanding a jury trial and financial damages.

The lawsuits are the first major civil actions taken against the Trump administration over its unprecedented deportation crackdowns in Minneapolis last winter, dubbed Operation Metro Surge.

The first lawsuit seeks damages for Good’s wrongful death under Minnesota law, citing claims of assault, battery, false imprisonment, negligence and intentional infliction of emotional distress.

The second lawsuit alleges a civil rights conspiracy among numerous defendants including the immigration officer and shooter Jonathon Ross, who was named alongside high-ranking Trump administration officials, including White House Deputy Policy Chief Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino and Trump’s longtime campaign adviser, Corey Lewandowski.

Good, a mother of three, was shot and killed in her car by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent in south Minneapolis when she and her wife joined one of the city’s daily demonstrations against masked and armed federal agents deployed to the city to arrest migrants for deportation.

Widespread cellphone footage taken by eyewitnesses captured the moment in which Good was killed, after agent Ross fired into the windshield, shooting her in the head, arm and torso.

Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defence and that Good had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism”.

In a statement posted on Truth Social at the time, Trump defended the deadly ICE shooting, saying that the reason those “incidents” were happening was that “the Radical Left is threatening, assaulting, and targeting our Law Enforcement Officers and ICE Agents on a daily basis”.

Days after the shooting, officials from the US Department of Justice, including then-Deputy Attorney Todd Blanche, blocked federal prosecutors from pursuing a criminal civil rights case against the agents involved in her killing, which prompted at least half a dozen of those prosecutors to resign in protest.

Minnesota sued the Trump administration in March to gain access to the evidence it gathered at the shooting scenes, but investigations stalled after the Justice Department halted its routine cooperation and evidence-sharing with the Minneapolis Police Department.

None of the agents involved in Good’s killing has faced any charges.

articles.title: US Supreme Court agrees to take up Trump’s ICE detention policy
articles.summary: The case is the latest dispute over US President Donald Trump’s sweeping immigration crackdown.
articles.body:
The United States Supreme Court has agreed to hear a case focused on the Trump administration’s policy requiring millions of undocumented immigrants to remain in detention while they fight deportation.

The case, accepted on Thursday by the justices, is the latest dispute over US President Donald Trump’s sweeping immigration crackdown to reach the nation’s highest court.

At issue is whether migrants already living in the US have a legal right to a hearing where a judge can decide whether they should be released on bond from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention while their deportation cases are pending.

In July 2025, the administration introduced new guidance directing federal immigration authorities to detain undocumented immigrants without a bond hearing for the duration of their deportation proceedings, which can last for years.

The new policy, which has divided lower courts, reverses a decades-old interpretation that allowed some immigrants in the US to be released while their cases were pending in immigration court, according to Reuters news agency.

Most US federal appeals courts have ruled that immigrants cannot be detained without a bond hearing. But the 5th and 8th US Circuit Courts of Appeals have found that immigrants accused of illegally entering and remaining in the country must remain detained while their deportation cases proceed.

Trump administration attorneys told the Associated Press the split is “disrupting the orderly administration of immigration law”.

“The result is an unworkable patchwork of inconsistent immigration enforcement, where aliens present without admission are subject to mandatory detention in some circuits but are entitled to bond hearings and often released in others,” the lawyers wrote.

The Supreme Court case stems from a 2nd US Circuit Court of Appeals ruling involving Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a Brazilian national who entered the US around 2004 or 2005.

Immigration officers arrested him in September 2025 while he was driving to work in the US state of Massachusetts. He was initially denied a bond hearing under the administration’s policy but was later released on bond, according to court documents cited by Reuters.

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), which is representing the plaintiffs, told the Associated Press the Trump administration is trying to deny bond hearings for immigrants apprehended within the US rather than limiting the restriction to noncitizens stopped at the border.

“Millions of noncitizens could be affected by the government’s new interpretation,” ACLU attorneys wrote.

The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments on Monday, when its new term starts.

articles.title: Patriots tight end Eli Raridon and wife announce death of newborn son
articles.summary: New England Patriots tight end Eli Raridon and his wife, Anna Raridon, announced the death of their newborn son, who they said in a social media post never went home after he was born.
articles.body: New England Patriots tight end Eli Raridon and his wife, Anna Raridon, announced the death of their newborn son, who they said in a social media post never went home after he was born. Their son, Peter James Raridon, was born on September 11th, according to an Instagram post on Wednesday from the couple sharing the news. In the caption of the post, the couple said they learned at their 20-week anatomy scan that their son was diagnosed with anencephaly, which the couple described as “a fatal condition in which he would not survive outside the womb.” According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, anencephaly is a condition in which a child is born missing parts of their brain and skull. The condition is fatal and there is no current cure or treatment. “While we are absolutely devastated that we were unable to bring our baby boy home, I am grateful to have loved him deeply, kept him safe, and had been his home for the past 9 months before he was called back to Heaven,” the couple wrote in the Instagram post. “Though his time with us was brief, his life still precious, his purpose still meaningful, and he will forever be a part of our story,” the post added. “I have loved you every second of your life & will miss you every second of mine. What a sweet sweet reunion ours will be.” Eli and Anna Raridon were married on May 25, 2025, and announced on March 31 that they were expecting. “half me, half you— fearfully & wonderfully made, thank you Jesus!!! baby Raridon arriving this fall,” the caption of the announcement post said. Eli Raridon was drafted to the New England Patriots in the third round of the 2026 draft. He previously played college football at Notre Dame University.

articles.title: An Iowa farmer gave about 2 acres to two wind turbines and related infrastructure; by 2021, the $25,000 annual lease was what he called the most profitable part of his corn-and-soybean farm
articles.summary: An Iowa corn and soybean farmer found that using less than two acres of his cropland for renewable energy equipment created the most reliable financial
articles.body: An Iowa corn and soybean farmer found that using less than two acres of his cropland for renewable energy equipment created the most reliable financial return across his entire property. According to a feature published by Progressive Farmer in April 2021, the farmer agreed to host two industrial wind turbines, along with access roads and electrical equipment. In return, the energy developer paid him $25,000 each year. This created a fixed income stream that was much more predictable than traditional commodity markets. The arrangement shows a wider economic shift across rural farming communities in the United States. Landowners are increasingly combining crop farming with clean energy production to protect themselves from market changes and rising production costs.Financial stability on the farmTraditional farming can expose producers to major financial swings caused by international trade policy, extreme weather and changing prices for fertilizer, seed and fuel. According to DTN analysis, yearly turbine lease payments provide a guaranteed income floor that is not affected by rainfall or commodity prices. Speaking to Progressive Farmer about how the deal affected his business, the Iowa farmer said the wind energy agreement produced the highest net return per square foot of any enterprise on his land. Grain crops require large yearly expenses for chemical treatments, diesel fuel and specialized harvesting machinery. Lease agreements, however, require almost no yearly costs from the property owner. The physical space used by the turbines is very small compared with the total farm. Modern commercial wind towers require about three-quarters of an acre each for the concrete base, transformer pad and gravel access road. The surrounding fields can still be used normally with standard farm equipment.Growing adoption across the MidwestIowa has become a major center for onshore wind development in the United States. Data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration shows that wind turbines generated more than 60% of Iowa's total electricity output in recent years. This was the highest share of wind power generation of any state. Farmers across the Midwest have increasingly used energy development as another source of income. CBS News reported in a June 2024 regional broadcast that wind energy companies in rural areas provide important revenue for older farmers. The payments have helped some property owners deal with older farm debts and keep their family land during difficult market periods. Long-term utility agreements typically last 20 to 30 years. They give landowners a long-term source of income, unlike short-term grain contracts, which can change with market conditions.Community revenue and infrastructure impactUtility-scale wind projects can provide more than direct payments to landowners. They also create tax revenue for local governments and public school districts in rural counties. According to research published by the American Clean Power Association, wind developers pay more than $1.5 billion each year in combined land lease payments and local property taxes across the country. Despite these economic benefits, some communities have resisted new wind projects.
